3	Answer semantics:
4	- hypothesis: "supported" = the evidence, taken together, supports the claim more than its rivals; "contradicted" = the evidence counts against it; "unknown" = the evidence does not discriminate, so the claim is live but unestablished.
5	- edge (a claimed link from one condition to another): "causal" = the evidence supports a causal link (for example temporal order plus mechanism plus covariation with the main rival ruled out, a natural experiment, or an intervention result); "association-only" = they co-occur or correlate in the evidence but causation is not established; "contradicted" = evidence counts against the link; "unknown" = evidence is insufficient even to show association.
6	- action: "preferred" = among the best next actions given the evidence; "acceptable" = reasonable but not among the best; "premature" = could be right if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed, but committing now is not justified; "harmful" = likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party, or disable a protective control.
7	- sufficiency (item SUFF): is the evidence sufficient to commit to the action you rank highest, where that action is substantive rather than merely evidence-gathering? "sufficient" or "insufficient". Concluding that no intervention is warranted counts as a substantive decision.

329	CASE OD2-HO-MISLEAD-2 (MISLEAD, technical): GET latency regression after gateway 5.8 at Tarnfield Object Storage
330	Setting: Quillon Cloud runs Tarnfield, a fictional object storage service. Stateless gateways terminate client requests, check request signatures, look up metadata and fetch object chunks from storage nodes. The fleet is organised as 12 cells across three regions (us-e, ap-s, eu-w). Gateway software ships through a release pipeline that posts to a shared change calendar. Storage-node settings are changed through a separate fleet configuration system.
331	Presenting request: The VP of Platform Engineering wants a decision today on rolling gateway 5.8 back to 5.7 across the fleet. You have been asked to assess what is driving the GET latency regression and which of the proposed actions should be taken. You may collect at most two items from the catalogue.
332	INITIAL EVIDENCE
333	E1 [stage S1] Priya Halvorsen, VP Platform Engineering, email to incident channel, 4 Nov 09:12 (leadership-account): GET p99 has been stuck near 300 ms since the gateway 5.8 rollout on the night of 2–3 Nov. Before that it was 90 ms. The dashboard shows it climbing as the rollout went out. 5.8 changed the read path, and gateway CPU is up 18%. I want a fleet-wide rollback to 5.7 today. Security has objected because of the signature fix, but customer latency comes first and we can re-ship the fix later. The storage and network teams have confirmed nothing of theirs is involved.
334	E2 [stage S1] Fleet latency dashboard export with deployment annotations (telemetry): Fleet GET p99, hourly average of 5-minute p99 values (ms), night of 2–3 Nov. Annotation: 'gateway 5.8 rollout 22:05–04:10 (us-e 22:05–23:30, ap-s 23:35–01:50, eu-w 02:30–04:10)'. 20:00 90; 21:00 91; 22:00 93; 23:00 139; 00:00 284; 01:00 291; 02:00 296; 03:00 301; 04:00 298; 05:00 297. Daily median p99: 1 Nov 90, 2 Nov 91, 4 Nov 296, 6 Nov 294, 8 Nov 297. The shared change calendar for 2–3 Nov has one entry: gateway 5.8 rollout.
335	E3 [stage S1] Gateway 5.8 release notes (approved 30 Oct) (change-record): Changes: (1) Fixes SEC-2291, a request-signature replay weakness reported by external auditors. Versions 5.7 and earlier remain exposed, and audit closure requires 5.8 across the fleet by 30 Nov. (2) Read path: parallel range-fetch fan-out raised from 4 to 8 for large objects. (3) TLS library upgrade. Known effect: gateway CPU +15–20% from the added signature checks. Rollback procedure: redeploy 5.7, about 4 hours across the fleet.
336	E4 [stage S1] Interview notes, storage platform manager, 4 Nov (manager-account): 'We pushed a routine compaction tuning change through the fleet config system on the evening of 2 Nov, because backlog alerts had been firing since about 31 Oct. Fleet config pushes don't go on the shared change calendar and never have. Compaction is background work and yields to client reads, so it can't be behind a read-latency problem. And to be clear, we never pause compaction. Once backlog passes about 15% of extents, read amplification climbs and nodes start running toward disk-full.'
337	E5 [stage S1] Network on-call handover note, 3 Nov 08:00 (staff-account): 'Elevated TCP retransmits on us-e spine-2 from 02:10 to 04:50 on 3 Nov, traced to a flapping optic. We replaced the optic at 04:50 and retransmits have been at baseline since. Nothing comparable in ap-s or eu-w. Gateway-to-storage round-trip time medians are 0.4–0.6 ms in all three regions, same as last week. We don't see a network angle on the GET latency issue.'
338	E6 [stage S1] Customer success note and traffic summary, 4 Nov (document): On 30 Oct Orrin Media began migrating its archive into Tarnfield, writing about 18 TB/day across all three regions. It is a background copy with a 15 Dec deadline and is currently ahead of schedule. Orrin's contract allows temporary ingest rate limits with 24 hours' notice, and their technical lead has said pacing is fine. Fleet traffic, 28 Oct to 4 Nov: GET requests/s rose 6%, gradually across the week. PUT requests/s rose 14%.

Unit and integration suites passed (2,318 tests). The range-fetch fan-out change applies to objects above 64 MiB. The signature check adds an HMAC verification and a nonce-cache lookup per request. Reviewer comment: 'possible CPU cost; no storage-side effect expected.' Integration tests run against an in-memory storage stub, not real storage nodes.

rulings.explanation: The task's own definition of causal accepts temporal order plus mechanism plus covariation with the main rival ruled out. All three are met. (1) Temporal order: C11 says disk utilisation crossed 90% within 5 minutes of the push in each cell, and C6 shows p99 onset 2–13 minutes after each push. (2) Mechanism with matching size: disk read queue wait rose by 196 ms (9→205), node-side service time (which excludes network) rose by 201 ms (61→262), and fleet p99 rose by about 205 ms. Queue wait is a direct part of node service time, so the extra latency is accounted for almost entirely by waiting on saturated disks. (3) Rivals excluded: C6 rules out gateway 5.8 through the aps-3 natural experiment (5.8 present, no push, no regression) and the euw-1 rollback test. E5 and C11 (time measured on the node) rule out the network, and E6/C6 rule out traffic growth (aps-3 had +7% traffic and no regression). The objection that nobody intervened on saturation directly does not hold, because the definition does not require an intervention. 'Association-only' would ignore the matching decomposition and the excluded rivals.

'Unknown' means the evidence cannot even show association. Here the evidence does show co-occurrence. Orrin's writes began 30 Oct (E6, C9, C11), the backlog grew from 3.1% to 11.2% over the same window (C11), PUT traffic rose 14% (E6), and the mechanism is plausible (about 18 TB/day of new writes creates compaction work). The definition of association-only explicitly includes 'co-occur', so this meets the bar. Causation is not established: the lifecycle-expiry sweep overlaps in time and also creates compaction work, and C11 says the backlog growth is not yet attributed by source. That rules out 'causal'. Nothing counts against the link, so 'contradicted' does not apply. That leaves association-only as the single fitting label. The overlap with the sweep is exactly why the link is not causal, not a reason to call it unknown.

A3 is worth doing only if Orrin's writes drive the backlog (R4), and R4 is only an association with an unexcluded rival (the sweep). That is the definition of premature. The revised C11 also removes the case for pacing now as a cheap hedge. The backlog is 4.0% and falling at 6 threads, so no growth needs slowing yet. Even after A2 restores 2 threads, the worst-case projection says the backlog cannot reach 15% before 13 Nov. The attribution job reports on 10 Nov, which leaves time to confirm R4 and still give the 24-hour contractual notice before any danger. The 'acceptable' argument (low cost, the contract allows it, the customer agreed) explains why A3 is not harmful. It does not make A3 justified now: constraining a customer on an unconfirmed attribution, with no urgency, is committing before the evidence is in. Premature is the only label that fits.

Premature needs the action's value to depend on a hypothesis that is still unconfirmed. A5 does not. The CPU increase is already established (E3 lists it as a known effect, C4 measures 34%→40%), and profiling it is useful for capacity planning whatever caused the incident. Its value also does not depend on H1, and H1 is contradicted anyway. A5 is low cost and does not weaken any protective control, so it is not harmful. It does nothing to resolve the incident, so it is not among the best actions (not preferred). The remaining label, acceptable, is the only defensible one.
